EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense lake effect snow band produced dangerous travel and near whiteout conditions. Snowfall totals exceeded a foot in portions of western Cass and Berrien counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A single band of heavy lake effect developed behind an arctic front during the morning hours of January 14th, becoming nearly stationary and intensifying during the late afternoon through early morning hours of January 15th. Snowfall rates of more than 2 inches per hour were reported with near zero visibility. Snowfall totals were heaviest across far western portions of Cass County, with a report of 17.0 inches at Barron Lake. There were innumerous slide-offs and crashes across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long duration snow event produced 3 to 6 inches of accumulation late January 24th into January 25th, heaviest during the morning hours of January 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow developed during the late evening hours of January 24th and continued through the early evening hours of January 25th. The snow accumulated to between 4 and 6 inches and was fluffy in nature as temperatures were in the single digits and teens. Roads were snow covered and slick with reports of accidents and slide-offs across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: System snow overspread southern Lower Michigan during the evening hours of January 18th which was followed by periods of lake effect snow on January 19th behind an arctic front. Storm total snowfall accumulations ranged from 2 to 6 inches across southwest Lower Michigan with the greatest amounts reported closer to Lake Michigan.  Strong winds coupled with the snow and blowing snow produced significant visibility reductions at times and hazardous travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light system snow during the late afternoon and evening of January 18th was followed by bands of lake effect snow. The combination of west wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph and the snowfall resulted in significant visibility reductions of less than one quarter of a mile at times due to snow and blowing snow. Storm total snow accumulations were in the 2 to 5 inch range. A report of 3.4 inches of snow was received 2.8 miles north northwest of Edwardsburg, MI. Numerous slide-offs and accidents were reported across the region. In addition, wind chills dropped to as cold as 15 below during the early morning hours of January 19th extending into early afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass entered the UP late on the 22nd, with very cold wind chills of -25F or lower persisting at times through the morning of the 26th. The coldest wind chills occurred during the mornings of the 23rd and 24th, when minimum values ranged from -30 to -55F in the central and western UP, and -25 to -25F in the eastern UP. For some areas in the central and western UP, this was the coldest 3 and 4 day stretch since January 2019. Numerous schools, businesses, and services were closed on Friday the 23rd and Saturday the 24th.||In addition to the cold temperatures, blizzard conditions accompanied the initial push of cold air during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd in the Keweenaw, with whiteout conditions leading to several traffic accidents and road closures. Another round of heavy accumulating lake effect snow occurred in the northeastern UP on the 23rd, with very low visibilities resulting in at least one road closure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds, accumulating snow, and cold temperatures resulted in blizzard conditions during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd. Key impacts: traffic accidents, transportation delays.

In addition, wind chills dropped to as cold as 15 below during the early morning hours of January 19th extending into early afternoon.

Strong lake effect snow showers occurred January 28 through January 29th, impacting Luce, Schoolcraft, and Alger counties in Upper Michigan. As the event progressed, a dominant lake effect band slowly progressed westward, which eventually focused impacts into Alger County. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals ranged from 5 to as much as 20 inches or more across the county, much of which was mixed with or solely sleet. Some freezing rain occurred as well. County offices were proactively closed for the 16th due to conditions. Road clearing in the county was slowed by the thick, dense sleet/snowpack overwhelming county trucks, requiring equipment repairs.

Both Detroit City Airport and Ann Arbor Airport recorded peak gusts of 71 mph during the height of the storm. The most intense winds occurred in the afternoon following the passage of a strong cold front, leaving around 200,000 DTE Energy customers without power at the peak of the event. Tragically, the storm claimed the life of a Huntington Woods public works employee, who was struck by a falling tree limb while working to clear a roadway during the evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Upwards of 22-25 inches of snow measured at cooperative observer sites at Tahquamenon Falls State Park and Paradise, respectively, with estimates of close to 30 inches in a few areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 6th, 2026, a lone supercell developed in La Porte County, IN and tracked northeast into Lower Michigan. The supercell moved through Cass, St Joseph, Branch, and Calhoun counties. NWS storm damage surveys from NWS Northern Indiana and NWS Grand Rapids found that the parent supercell spawned 4 tornadoes across Lower Michigan, ranging from EF-0 to EF-3 intensity. There were numerous reports called in to our office and videos posted on social media by storm chasers, broadcast media, trained spotters, and the public confirming tornado damage in Edwardsburg, Three Rivers, and Union City. The north side of Union Lake in Union City was one of the hardest hit areas with numerous homes taking on significant damage and trees sheared off. Several businesses in the city of Three Rivers also sustained notable damage. Unfortunately, there were multiple fatalities and injuries across Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Picture shared on social media of a hailstone larger than a quarter.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The most intense and deadly tornado of the cyclic tornadic|supercell touched down in northwest Branch county, northwest of|Union Lake between Blossom Rd and Mendon Rd. This tornado was|well photographed from multiple angles, and it quickly turned|into a multi-vortex wedge. After destroying a pole barn and|damaging a residence, the tornado deposited a 500 gallon propane|tank in a field. Drone footage also showed ground scouring in the|same field. The tornado continued northeast and caused the most|widespread and intense damage along Prairie Rose Ln. Every|residence along this stretch was either heavily damaged or|completely destroyed. Tragically, three individuals lost their|lives here when their manufactured homes were lofted and tossed.|One of these trailers was well anchored and tossed approximately|100 yards, badly twisting the frame. Numerous vehicles were also|tossed in this area. The maximum peak intensity of 160 mph was|estimated to be at the corner of Tuttle Rd and Prairie Rose Ln.|This 2 story block home was completely destroyed. Construction|quality and older building codes of all homes in this area|contributed to their failure and precluded the survey team from|being able to rate higher than an EF-3. The tornado continued off|to the northeast into Union City producing EF-1 to EF2 damage|along the way before dissipating at the Branch/Calhoun county|line. Special thanks to the various subject matter experts on the|Quick Response Team that helped NWS Northern Indiana determine|this tornado's intensity.

The supercell moved through Cass, St Joseph, Branch, and Calhoun counties. NWS storm damage surveys from NWS Northern Indiana and NWS Grand Rapids found that the parent supercell spawned 4 tornadoes across Lower Michigan, ranging from EF-0 to EF-3 intensity. There were numerous reports called in to our office and videos posted on social media by storm chasers, broadcast media, trained spotters, and the public confirming tornado damage in Edwardsburg, Three Rivers, and Union City. The north side of Union Lake in Union City was one of the hardest hit areas with numerous homes taking on significant damage and trees sheared off. Several businesses in the city of Three Rivers also sustained notable damage. Unfortunately, there were multiple fatalities and injuries across Lower Michigan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Near-blizzard conditions were observed at KCIU on the 16th, with winds gusting 25-35mph and visibilities of a quarter mile or less off and on for several hours. Snowfall totals across the county were around 10 inches in the city of Sault Ste. Marie, MI to as high as 31 inches near Pickford. State offices were proactively closed for the 16th due to the anticipated conditions. Michigan State Police rescued an escaped horse on M-129 near Sault Ste. Marie during the near-blizzard conditions, but all parties, including the horse, were uninjured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across Southeast Michigan during the late afternoon and early evening of April 4. This triggered two lines of thunderstorms that caused pockets of damage south of I-94. The most significant storm occurred in Wayne County, producing an EF-1 tornado in Van Buren Township. The system also dumped 1 to 3 inches of rain, with some areas seeing up to 4 inches. Because the region had already received 3 to 5 inches over the previous five days, these additional downpours caused the Tittabawassee, Clinton, and Flint rivers to overflow. In addition, significant localized flooding occurred on already saturated ground, with the hardest-hit area being northwest Oakland County, specifically in and around Holly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees downed in the vicinity of Piehl Rd., Summerfield Rd., Erie Rd., and St. Anthony Rd. Damage to two homes reported on Piehl Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A heavy band of lake effect snow clipped portions of Huron and Sanilac counties late on February 6th into the early morning hours of February 7th. While the event produced localized snow accumulations of 3 inches, northwest winds gusting 40 to 50 mph contributed to significant blowing and drifting snow. Whiteout conditions were reported, especially closer to the Lake Huron shoreline and in rural areas. Numerous vehicles were stranded due to whiteout conditions. Bitterly cold conditions also settled in as the heavy snow and strong winds arrived. Wind chill values fell to around 10 to 12 below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-phased system brought a combination of system and lake enhanced snow to southwest Lower Michigan Saturday night into early Sunday morning followed by more organized lake effect snow showers late Sunday into Monday.  This prolonged snow event coupled with gusty north to northwest winds lead to hazardous travel conditions and numerous slide-offs and accidents across southwest Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of system and lake enhanced snow Saturday night into Sunday morning, followed by a more organized lake effect snow phase Sunday afternoon through midday Monday. In addition to the snow, north to northwest winds gusting to 30 to 35 mph resulted in significant blowing and drifting snow along with periods of significantly reduced visibilities.  Numerous slide-offs and accidents were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass entered the UP late on the 22nd, with very cold wind chills of -25F or lower persisting at times through the morning of the 26th. The coldest wind chills occurred during the mornings of the 23rd and 24th, when minimum values ranged from -30 to -55F in the central and western UP, and -25 to -25F in the eastern UP. For some areas in the central and western UP, this was the coldest 3 and 4 day stretch since January 2019. Numerous schools, businesses, and services were closed on Friday the 23rd and Saturday the 24th.||In addition to the cold temperatures, blizzard conditions accompanied the initial push of cold air during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd in the Keweenaw, with whiteout conditions leading to several traffic accidents and road closures. Another round of heavy accumulating lake effect snow occurred in the northeastern UP on the 23rd, with very low visibilities resulting in at least one road closure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds, accumulating snow, and cold temperatures resulted in blizzard conditions during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd. US-41 was closed in at least two spots north of Houghton due to traffic accidents and whiteout conditions. There was an 8-car pileup near the Houghton County Airport, and multiple smaller accidents. Key impacts: traffic accidents, transportation delays, road closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: SW flow lake effect snow developed late in the day on the 18th, and a mesolow dropped SSE across the area on the morning of the 19th, crossing from Leelanau County to near Grayling through the morning hours. A strong NW flow lake effect band developed in its wake with flow ultimately shifting to the WNW in the late afternoon/evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spotter reported 9 inches of snow fell between midnight and 9am on the 19th, with a 48-hr total of 16.7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Anomalous cold air settled into the eastern US for late January, with the coldest period for the Upper Great Lakes from the night of Jan 22nd through the morning of the 24th. Actual air temperatures struggling to break 0 degrees Fahrenheit, combined with winds gusting as high as 15-25mph at times, resulted in extreme cold apparent temperatures of -15 to -25F, and -25 to -35F during the overnight hours on the 22nd into the 23rd, and the 23rd into the 24th. The 23rd into the 24th was the coldest of the two nights. Strong gusty winds and some snowfall resulted in significant blowing and drifting snow, reducing visibilities to whiteout conditions at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Apparent temperatures at KMCD, Mackinac Island AWOS, as low as -34F on the night of the 22nd-23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wing of warm advection snow overspread the area during the day of the 10th, with a mesolow crossing the Leelanau Peninsula and tracking near the M-72 corridor during the evening, leading to localized snowfall totals as high as 10-12 inches where N to NNW flow lake enhancement came into play across parts of Leelanau, Benzie, and Grand Traverse Counties, as well as into the Kalkaska county area. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second in a round of back-to-back winter storms impacted portions of the UP from the early morning hours of February 20th through the early morning hours of February 21st. The precipitation started as freezing rain for much of the central UP, resulting in slippery surfaces, before changing to heavy, wet snow. The combination of the snow and freezing rain resulted in treacherous travel conditions and prompted the closure of many schools and businesses on Friday the 20th. Total snowfall ranged from around 5 inches in southern Iron and Dickinson Counties to near a foot in portions of the north-central UP and Keweenaw.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing rain of up to 0.2 occurred, followed by heavy, wet snow of 3-5. Key impacts: travel delays, school closures, traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong lake effect snow showers occurred January 28 through January 29th, impacting Luce, Schoolcraft, and Alger counties in Upper Michigan. As the event progressed, a dominant lake effect band slowly progressed westward, which eventually focused impacts into Alger County. Heavy snowfall was observed, with snowfall rates of 1 inch per hour or greater and gusty northwest winds contributing to blowing snow and reduced visibilities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Chatham Cooperative Observer (CEFM4) observed 8 inches of snow between 0800 1/28 and 1/29. Impacts for this event began on 1/27, when it was also reported that a hill along M-28 in Wetmore was closed because a traffic incident involving a semi. Frequent whiteouts were also reported on M-28 between Harvey and Munising and Alger County Sheriff advised that people should stay home and not travel unless absolutely necessary. It was reported that Munising schools had closed early. Key impacts: Difficult to dangerous travel.

Total snowfall ranged from around 5 inches in southern Iron and Dickinson Counties to near a foot in portions of the north-central UP and Keweenaw.
